column5: Probably yes. Slow response of employment to demand doesn't seem to be due to other factors. But no hard evidence and still some uncertainty
column8: Theory strongly suggests yes. But with low employment growth and the supplement set to expire, the hoped-for impact may be small or absent.

column5: "Major" is probably too strong, but with COVID improving and labor demand rebounding, UI benefit levels matter more now than before.
column8: I expect wages in low wage, higher turnover jobs to rise, but firms will not make big wage changes in response to a temporary policy.

column5: Since there's no evidence on this Q yet, only the WSJ editorial page can be certain that it constitutes a major disincentive to work!
I haven't seen a study that is current.
the "major" part makes me uncertain.
$300 of extra money per week is quite meaningful to a low wage worker.  Certainly enough to affect decisions.
column8: Too complex to guess.  Workers can wait for a good opportunity.  But long term unemployed people often have bad opportunities.

column5: I go for "minor disincentive." More important are childcare responsibilities, fear of COVID in jobs with close personal contact.
column8: I go for "economically marginal" instead of "economically meaningful," following the logic of my answer to the first question.

column5: Not likely "major"
column8: labor supply increases, wages rise?  But wages may rise along with price inflation.

column5: It depends. In sectors where demand has not yet recovered, the $300 is not the issue. Where demand has recovered, the disincentive may exist
column8: IFF they get re-employed, probably yes. By how much is uncertain, depends on the industry and state.

column5: So far slow hiring is not really correlated w/UI generosity either across sectors or across states. Once things are “normal” again, then yes
column8: Maybe for some but not overall (yet)

column5: Only for people eligible for benefits
I don't think we know enough about it. Fears of getting Covid may be a more important factor.
The existing evidence is now dated but shows that moral hazard is not large. That could be changing but no evidence yet that it has.
column8: I want to believe this but little evidence from the US that this is the case.
Higher UI benefits allows workers to spend more time looking for a good job, in terms of wages or other job characteristics.

column5: How many think with the uncertainty about how reopening will proceed and the risk of reversals and another layoff, why take a job now?
There will be some adverse effect on employment, just not clear how much
column8: Depends on how sticky wages are.

column5: major too strong, but significant
column8: could add a few basis points to wage inflation
Extensive unemployment ins. empirical evidence not able to show such wage effects. This is a much bigger experiment that we will learn from.

column5: Anecdotal cases of benefit recipients declining work will abound, but the evidence is that the effect is not major.
column8: It will be difficult to distinguish this effect from the effect of looming inflation.

column5: It is a disincentive but not sure about major
column8: Higher UI increases workers bargaining position and also allows searching for better matches. Not sure about economically meaningful amount.

column5: Clearly a disincentive, but major?  Compared with the effect of schools being closed?
Many workers are still get more in UI than their old wage.
column8: There is no evidence that higher UI raises reemployment wages (perhaps surprisingly)

column5: "Major" is probably too strong, but it does permit some workers to search more/longer for better jobs.
